answer:
So I had a chance meeting recently with a very senior IT leader at one of the world’s largest tech leaders (think Google, Amazon, etc.). We met for coffee during a conference we both were attending, and talked about … our kids! It was great catching up with him. But then he turned it around on me:
“Jason, you’re so passionate about your little start-ups that sell into enterprises. How do they get deals?”
I didn’t know exactly what he meant, but when I thought back, I realized his question wasn’t entirely fair. Or even correct. And yet, I did see a lot of truth there too.
The thing is, almost every successful startup I’ve ever worked with has sold its first $1m+ deal before it had 10 employees. In fact, most of them got past Initial Traction after just 5-6 employees. So yes, you can sell large corporate customers to startups with < 20 employees. More than often, you need to. There’s no other choice. You don’t have enough cash or people.
But there is a social contract here. Let’s talk about it.
The Social Contract:
In the enterprise, folks like SAP, Oracle, Microsoft, IBM, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Adobe, etc. all spend hundreds of millions, if not billions, on software each year. All that money goes through procurement processes, RFPs, committees, and more. Big Tech itself spends tens of billions on software annually. Again, much of it goes through strict business processes.
It’s hard to imagine any Fortune 500 company buying more than say, $250k-$300k worth of software without going through some sort of formal evaluation and selection process. Probably even smaller ones would want to go through something similar.
Even Facebook only bought two new vendors last quarter. Two.

answer: Can an 8-Person StartUp Sell to a CIO? Yes — If You Understand The Social Contract In today’s business landscape, it seems impossible that an eight-person startup could successfully sell to a large enterprise with thousands of employees like Google. But I’ve seen it happen multiple times, and each time it has been a remarkable experience. These deals aren’t just wins for the startup—they’re often game-changers for both parties involved. Here’s what makes them tick. Understanding the Purchasing Guidelines First things first: any successful purchase within a company follows strict guidelines, including approval levels, vendor selection processes, and financial constraints. This isn’t some mythical creature—it’s standard operating procedure at every major tech firm out there. When you approach an enterprise sale, you need to speak their language and navigate these guidelines effectively. Building Trust Through Relationships Let me tell you something most people miss: relationships matter more than revenue when selling to enterprises. At Adobe Sign (formerly EchoSign), we focused heavily on building long-term partnerships rather than chasing short-term gains. We made sure our customers felt valued beyond just getting the software they needed. For example, one of my biggest clients was willing to pay $300K+ per year because they saw us as partners—not just vendors. They knew if we failed, they’d lose access to critical functionality during peak season. That kind of commitment takes years to build but pays dividends in the end. Being Authentic and Transparent About Your Capabilities It sounds obvious, but too many startups try to fake it until they make it when dealing with larger organizations. Don’t do this

answer:
So we're all here at Dreamforce, and I want to start off with just one question. How many of you know anyone that has sold anything into the enterprise before?
Just raise your hand if you've ever done it, whether it was pre-sales, post-sales, etc. It doesn't matter. But I'm guessing there's no more than maybe 10 people out of 1,000 of us today. We'll see. So I wanted to come together and give some thoughts because we do now have a number of $100m plus unicorns in our portfolio and we've been doing enterprise software since '07, so we had to figure out how to get to those folks. Because they're hard. They're hard to sell to. And I think most importantly, they need help. In fact, the whole theme for my next book will be "SaaStr Unicorns". What did they do differently? Why were they different? How did they win? And I came up with what I call the social contract between a startup and a customer. This is something I learned after being in sales myself. There are only two types of customers that really matter in SaaS: the CEO, and the CIO. That's where the money comes from. It does not always come from the VPs. It does not always come from marketing. Those guys are important, but ultimately, they don't make the decisions. So let me break down a little bit what the CEO-CIO relationship is like, because this is going to be very helpful when we talk about the sales motion later.

We
last looked in on Monday.com at $240m ARR
, but it’s grown so incredibly quickly, and so effectively, it’s worth checking in again at $400,000,000 in ARR.
Because at $400,000,000 in ARR …  Monday is growing a stunning 91% (!) year-over-year.  Goodness gracious!
5 Interesting Learnings:

#1.  Revenue up 91%, Customer Count Up “Just” 34%.  The math of going upmarket
.  I personally get a little worried when this ratio falls below 2:1, if only because sometimes upsell can mask lower growth in new accounts.  The real story with Monday is going upmarket.  $50k+ customers are up 200%, to 793 from 264 a year ago.  That’s a key driver to Monday’s hyper-growth as it approaches $500,000,000 in ARR.
#2.  10+ Users the Sweet Spot now
.  As part of going upmarket, Monday’s 10+ seat customers are now 72% of total revenue, up from 63% just a year ago.  Asana has seen similar dynamics, but Monday seems to be going upmarket even faster than Asana.

#7.  Monday.com is growing 68% (!) at $550m in ARR.  No SMB deceleration here!
Not much, at least.  Monday’s growth has slowed a little bit, but in absolute terms, the growth is just incredible even now.

.
